title: Witness casts doubt on officers' story
subtitle: Const. Steve Darnley's partner testified in day four of the coroner's inquest into the police shooting death of Duane Christian
article: A woman living in an apartment building next to where 15-year-old Duane Christian was shot dead by police, testified Thursday that she awoke that day to the sound of two male voices yelling at each other just before she heard several gunshots.
"I wanna go, I wanna go, just let me go," Joanne Blake said she heard a young male voice say, followed by an older man saying: "You're not going anywhere, I'm not letting you go."
Blake, who heard the exchange from her bed, said it was repeated for as long as five minutes before she heard the gunshots.
Christian was fatally shot in the arm and chest by Const. Steve Darnley shortly before 5 a.m. on June 20, 2006, while the teen was driving a stolen van in the parking lot of a Scarborough high rise.
Darnley said he had to shoot the teen, who he believed was going to run over his partner, Const. Rowena Edey, after the officers had confronted him in the roundabout area of the parking lot.

The Special Investigations Unit, a civilian agency that investigates all incidents of serious injury or death involving police, cleared the officer of any criminal culpability two months after the incident, saying he was justified in shooting Christian in order to protect his partner.
Christian's family, however, has launched a landmark $2 million negligence lawsuit against the SIU, alleging their investigation was incompetent.
A coroner's inquest is probing all of the circumstances surrounding the teen's death, but not the SIU's investigation.

Blake's testimony contradicts what Darnley previously told the inquest - that no words were exchanged between him and Christian - and both police officers' assertion that the incident happened so fast, there was little time to consider any option other than to shoot the van's driver.

Toronto Police Association lawyer Peter Thorning was quick to cast doubt on the credibility of Blake's memory, suggesting she was likely dazed after just waking up, and also pointing to discrepancies between some of the information she provided to investigators on the day in question and what she recalled Thursday.
"You've basically forgotten about this whole incident, haven't you?" he said.
Thorning also suggested Blake's memory had been influenced by news reports and conversations with neighbours.
Blake maintained that while she didn't remember all of the details surrounding the incident, she was sure of what she heard that morning.
Edey, who also testified Thursday, said she was "absolutely certain" Blake's evidence was untrue, although she also said she experienced "auditory exclusion" during the incident.
Edey said she made three attempts to move out of the van's path as it drove toward her, but the driver was deliberately tracking her movements and was intending to run her over.
"I'd done everything reasonable to get out of his way," she said, adding that she would have been dead if Darnley hadn't intervened.
But the lawyer representing Christian's mother said Edey's recollection is inconsistent with tire marks left by the van and the angle at which it struck a nearby tree.
"I'm suggesting to you that nothing could have happened the way you remember it happening," said Peter Rosenthal, who suggested that Christian was actually trying to flee the parking lot.
"That night he tried to kill me, that's all I can tell you," Edey said.
Edey continues her testimony Friday.
